overview: Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, and also took several governorships, according to AP, CBS News and other outlets. President Trump said he would accept the results. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul won a second full term and city voters approved all five ballot proposals from Mayor Mamdani's charter commission. Abroad, Trump said the US will end about $4 billion a year in military aid to Israel after this year, Russia struck a Ukrainian aid site as the US announced talks in Abu Dhabi, and Spain's transport minister resigned after a deadly train crash.

stories.headline: Democrats win control of both the House and the Senate in the midterms
stories.summary: Outlets including CBS News, the Associated Press and PBS NewsHour report that Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, is in line to become speaker. The new Congress is sworn in in early January.
stories.why_it_matters: Divided government means Republicans can no longer pass bills or confirm nominees on their own for the last two years of Trump's term, and Democrats gain power to investigate the administration.
stories.background: All 435 House seats, 35 of 100 Senate seats and 36 governorships were on the ballot. Republicans entered the night with majorities in both chambers, which allowed them to pass a large tax-cut law in 2025. President Trump campaigned heavily and encouraged voters to treat the election as a verdict on him, and exit polls showed concern about the economy and prices. Democrats needed a net gain of three House seats and four Senate seats to take control.

facts.text: CBS News projected that Democrats won both the House and the Senate.
PBS NewsHour reported Democrats won the House in addition to the Senate, calling it a rebuke of Republican governance in Washington.
Axios, citing AP projections, said Republicans lost Senate seats in South Carolina, Kansas and Texas as well as House seats nationwide.
Democrats are in line to hold the House majority when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3, according to France 24.

NPR reported Jeffries, who would be the first Black speaker, said voters had sent a message to end extremism and corruption, and has vowed to focus on affordability and holding the administration accountable.
Axios reported Democrats won House districts that Trump carried by double digits.
Exact final seat totals were not given in the ingested articles; some races were still being counted.

framing.note: Leads on voters rejecting Trump's agenda and Democratic leverage over him.
Leads on inflation and the Iran war as reasons voters punished the GOP.
Treats it as a GOP wipeout and puts Trump's role as face of the campaign first.

stories.headline: Democrats flip Senate seats in Texas, North Carolina, Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina
stories.summary: Outlets report Democrats took Republican-held Senate seats in at least seven states, including several that Trump won in 2024. Democrats also held Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won reelection, and Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed won the open seat.
stories.why_it_matters: The Senate confirms judges and cabinet officials and can block legislation, so the results shape who gets appointed and what laws pass in the next two years.
stories.background: Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into the election, so Democrats needed a net gain of four seats. Open seats in North Carolina (Thom Tillis not running), Michigan and Iowa gave Democrats openings. In Maine, Troy Jackson became the nominee in July after Graham Platner withdrew. In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico faced Attorney General Ken Paxton in what the Guardian called the most expensive race of the cycle.

facts.text: Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in Texas, which PBS NewsHour described as the first Democratic statewide win in Texas since 1994.
Roy Cooper defeated Michael Whatley in North Carolina, CBS News projected, flipping a seat after Sen. Thom Tillis chose not to run.
Annie Andrews defeated Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina, a state Trump won three times by double digits, according to PBS and CBS.
Troy Jackson defeated five-term Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, per NBC News, NPR and AP.
Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa; Axios said the win sealed Democratic control of the Senate.
Adam Hamilton defeated Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, the first Democratic Senate win there in 94 years, per NPR and AP.
Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, per NBC News and CBS News.
Jon Ossoff won reelection in Georgia, per Reuters and AP.
Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan and will be the first Muslim U.S. senator, per the Guardian and France 24.
The Financial Times reported Elon Musk had put about $47 million toward Paxton's campaign.

framing.note: Washington Free Beacon calls El-Sayed's win a radical turn and stresses accusations about his associates; others lead with the historic first.
Guardian leads on the history of the win and Islamophobic attacks from Republicans.
Fox News frames Kansas as a historic upset for Republicans, with limited focus on why.
FT frames the Texas result as a blow to Elon Musk, who funded Paxton.

stories.headline: Democrats win governor's races in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Nevada
stories.summary: Democrats won several governorships that Republicans held or targeted, including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, and held Georgia. Republican Byron Donalds won Florida. Several winners are the first of their group to hold the office in their state.
stories.why_it_matters: Governors run state budgets, Medicaid, schools and election administration, so these results affect services and voting rules in some of the largest states.
stories.background: Thirty-six governorships were on the ballot. Ohio's Mike DeWine, Georgia's Brian Kemp and Iowa's governor were not on the ballot because of term limits or retirement. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott and Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo ran for reelection. Many of these races were also tied to national themes such as the cost of living and Trump's standing.

facts.text: Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the first Latina and first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years, per PBS NewsHour and AP.
Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, per NBC News and AP.
Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Rick Jackson in Georgia and is the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state, per The Hindu and Daily Maverick (Reuters).
Aaron Ford unseated Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada, per NPR and NBC News.
Rob Sand won Iowa's governor race, the first Democrat elected there since 2006, per CBS News and PBS.
Republican Byron Donalds, backed by Trump, was elected Florida's first Black governor, per BBC News.

framing.note: Fox News frames Ohio as the end of a 20-year GOP hold on the governor's office.
Daily Caller emphasizes Ramaswamy's spending of more than $80 million.
NPR groups the governors' wins as history-making firsts.

stories.headline: Trump responds to Republican midterm losses
stories.summary: Outlets report that Trump said he would accept the midterm results and posted about the causes of Republican losses. Accounts differ on what he blamed. Fox News reported he pledged to veto Democratic bills he called insane.
stories.why_it_matters: How the president responds to a Democratic Congress affects whether the two sides can pass spending bills and other must-pass legislation.
stories.background: Trump made himself the face of the Republican midterm campaign and repeatedly urged voters to act as if he were on the ballot. His approval rating had fallen amid concern about prices and the war with Iran, which has raised gas prices. Democrats now control both chambers and can block his legislation, subpoena officials and review his nominees.

facts.text: Reuters, citing the New York Times, reported Trump said he is willing to accept the midterm results.

stories.headline: Supreme Court hears Catholic preschools' challenge to Colorado program rules
stories.summary: The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday in a case over Catholic preschools that were excluded from Colorado's state-funded preschool program. CNN and the Wall Street Journal report that the conservative justices appeared sympathetic to the schools. A ruling is pending.
stories.why_it_matters: The decision could decide whether religious schools that take public money must follow state anti-discrimination rules on enrolling children of same-sex couples.
stories.background: Colorado's universal preschool program requires participating providers to follow a nondiscrimination policy that covers sexual orientation and gender identity. Catholic parishes, represented by the Becket Fund, say the rule forces them to act against their beliefs, and the Tenth Circuit ruled for the state. The case is St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, which the justices agreed to hear in April. The Trump administration's Solicitor General sided with the parishes.

facts.text: The Supreme Court heard a challenge by Catholic preschools to their exclusion from a Colorado-funded program, per AP and ABC News.
The Wall Street Journal reported conservative justices suggested the preschools should be eligible for taxpayer funds without complying with the nondiscrimination rule.
CNN reported the court appeared prepared to rule that publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples.
The Tenth Circuit rejected the preschools' argument, and the U.S. Solicitor General urged the court to stop Colorado's exclusion.

framing.note: CNN centers the effect on children of same-sex couples.
New York Sun uses the plaintiffs' phrase 'Catholics Need Not Apply' and centers religious exclusion.
WSJ centers the justices' sympathy for the schools and the funding question.

stories.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to intervene in California ballot count
stories.summary: The Japan Times reports the Supreme Court acted quickly on the eve of the election to reject an attempt by Trump to intervene in California's ballot count. Only one ingested outlet covers it.
stories.why_it_matters: It affects whether California counts ballots from voters the federal government has questioned and shows how the courts are handling election disputes.
stories.background: The Justice Department sued to keep California from counting about 20,000 ballots from voters it says are suspected noncitizens. California says voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury when they register. A Ninth Circuit panel rejected the department's request, and it was expected to go to the Supreme Court.

facts.text: The Japan Times reported the justices acted with remarkable speed to shut down Trump's attempt to intervene in California's ballot count on the eve of the election.
The Justice Department sought to have California set aside about 20,000 voters' ballots, and the Ninth Circuit rejected the request, per Democracy Docket.

stories.headline: State ballot measures: abortion rights gain in some states, California rejects billionaire tax
stories.summary: Voters in several states decided abortion, redistricting and tax measures. Virginia and Nevada approved abortion-rights amendments, Missouri rejected a ban and Idaho rejected a rights measure. Reports say California voters rejected the billionaire tax.
stories.why_it_matters: Abortion access and state taxes in these states now depend on the outcomes, which change what residents can do and pay.
stories.background: Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, abortion rules have been set state by state, often through ballot questions. Missouri voters legalized abortion in 2024, and this year's measure tied a ban to a ban on transgender treatment for minors. California's Proposition 40 proposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of people worth over $1 billion, mainly to replace federal health funding cuts.

facts.text: Missouri voters rejected a measure that would have re-imposed an abortion ban, NPR reported.
Virginia voters approved an abortion amendment, per the Daily Caller and National Review.
Nevada approved an amendment protecting abortion until viability, per Decision Desk HQ via The Hill.
Idaho voters rejected a measure to legalize abortion until viability, per The Hill and NBC News.
California voters rejected Prop 40 and a voter ID requirement, per The Center Square.
AP and France 24 reported voters backed abortion rights and rejected Trump-backed redistricting in ballot measures.

framing.note: Daily Caller emphasizes the Catholic Church's failed campaign.
NPR emphasizes that the Missouri ban was coupled with a ban on transgender treatment for minors.
New York Post stresses wealthy residents leaving and spending against Prop 40.

stories.headline: Trump says US will stop about $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel after this year
stories.summary: President Trump said on Election Day that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed the US will end roughly $4 billion in yearly funding to Israel after 2026, while continuing to sell it weapons. The Wall Street Journal reported that the two governments had discussed phasing out grants but that his remarks point to a much faster timeline. No joint statement was in the digest.
stories.why_it_matters: US military grants to Israel are a long-running part of the federal budget and of Middle East security planning. An abrupt end would shift costs and decisions to Israel and make the aid a live issue for the new Congress.
stories.background: The US gives Israel about $3.8 billion a year in military aid under a ten-year agreement that runs to 2028. Netanyahu has said publicly that Israel wants to wean itself off that aid over roughly a decade. The US and Israel have been fighting alongside each other in a war against Iran this year, and Israel policy has become a divisive issue inside both US parties. Trump made his announcement as US midterm voting was under way.

facts.text: Trump said on Tuesday he made a deal with Netanyahu under which Washington would stop $4bn in annual funding to Israel after this year but keep selling it weapons, Reuters reported.
Deutsche Welle reported Trump added that Democratic candidates were using US military support for Israel against Republicans in the midterms.
The New York Times reported Trump described the arrangement as an agreement reached months ago.
The Wall Street Journal reported the US and Israel had discussed phasing out grants, but that Trump's comments suggest it could happen far faster than expected.
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said the announcement shows 'how bad the polling is' on the issue, The Hill reported.

stories.headline: Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site kills at least 31 as US announces Abu Dhabi talks
stories.summary: A Russian strike on an aid distribution site and shelter in Komyshuvakha, in southern Ukraine, killed at least 31 people with dozens missing, according to reports. Russia launched a large drone and missile barrage the same night. Hours later the US said peace talks with Russia and Ukraine would resume in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, which the Kremlin confirmed.
stories.why_it_matters: The strike is one of the deadliest on civilians in the war, and the barrage hit Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter. The talks are the first US-mediated round since February.
stories.background: Russia has been at war with Ukraine since its 2022 invasion. US-led peace efforts were suspended in February, Axios reported, because of the war in Iran. US envoy Steve Witkoff announced the new round as working-level talks on security arrangements and de-escalation. European leaders such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz say Russia must show it is serious about a ceasefire.

facts.text: NPR reported the death toll had reached 29 with 48 missing; President Zelenskyy said Russia launched 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions.
The Hindu and the Wall Street Journal reported at least 31 dead, with dozens missing at the site in Komyshuvakha.
Witkoff announced US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
The Kremlin confirmed the talks, The Hindu reported.
Merz said Russia must show it is serious about a ceasefire at the talks, Reuters reported.
Reuters reported Russia bombarded Ukraine's power grid before the talks.

stories.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island; Trump says no immediate plan for more
stories.summary: The US carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island late Monday, and Iran said it shot down US drones. On Tuesday Trump told the Financial Times the US has no immediate plan to strike Iran but is ready if needed, and later said the war was a factor in Republican midterm losses. Reuters also reported Iran's Revolutionary Guards saying four tankers caught fire after hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of the world's oil, so fighting or mines there can move fuel prices and shipping costs. The outcome of US-Iran talks affects whether the war resumes.
stories.background: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran this year, and a ceasefire and talks, with Qatar as a mediator, have been on and off. Control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been a central dispute. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have said diplomacy is progressing even as strikes continue. The New York Times reported Iranian officials said they could reopen the strait within two days as part of a deal.

facts.text: The US launched limited strikes on Qeshm Island late Monday, reportedly targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, hours after Vance voiced optimism about a deal, the Guardian reported.
Iran said it shot down US drones after the reported strikes, per the Washington Times headline.
Iran's president said a return to war benefits 'no one', The Hindu reported.
Trump told the Financial Times the US has no immediate plan to strike Iran, saying 'We seem to be getting everything we want'.
Reuters reported Iran's IRGC said four tankers were ablaze after hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump told Fox News 'a part of it was Iran' when asked about his party's midterm defeat, France 24 reported.
The New York Times reported a Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran Monday and that Iranian officials spoke of progress toward reopening the strait.

stories.summary: Indonesia detained senior police officials and the president's chief of staff, a former national police chief, over alleged illegal wiretapping of President Prabowo Subianto and others. stories.headline: South Africans vote in local elections seen as a test for the ANC
stories.summary: Voters across South Africa's nine provinces cast ballots Wednesday in local elections. The Guardian reported the African National Congress is on course for a bruising result amid anger over water outages and power cuts. stories.background: The ANC has led South Africa since the end of white minority rule in 1994 but lost its national majority in 2024 and now governs in coalition. stories.summary: U.S. stock futures fell at first as Democrats won key races, then recovered after President Trump said he would accept the results, according to Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal. Treasury yields and the dollar fell and gold rose above $4,000 an ounce, Bloomberg reported. Analysts quoted by the Financial Times said divided government reduces policymaking risk.

Investors had been watching the vote for its possible effect on taxes, spending, tariffs and the AI-driven stock rally. stories.headline: Binance says fake job interviews led to $6.3 billion hack
stories.summary: Binance said Tuesday that an engineer was lured into fake job interviews that began a months-long attack ending in the theft of about $6.3 billion, according to BBC, Axios and NPR. stories.background: Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. Its roughly $6.3 billion loss is described by outlets as the biggest crypto theft on record. stories.headline: Euro zone inflation hits 4% as oil eases and central banks tighten
stories.summary: Euro zone inflation rose to 4% in October, the highest in three years and driven by energy prices, CNBC reported, with a European Central Bank rate rise looming. Australia raised rates to an 18-year high on Tuesday, CNBC reported. Oil fell to about $103 on an unconfirmed report of Middle East diplomacy, the Financial Times reported.
stories.why_it_matters: Energy-driven inflation raises prices for fuel, food and heating and pushes central banks toward higher interest rates and loan costs.
stories.background: Oil prices have risen sharply during the conflict involving Iran, which has raised energy costs worldwide. Central banks that had cut rates are now facing higher inflation. Australia's central bank has raised rates five times this year. Traders are watching whether Trump pursues diplomacy or renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms.

Deutsche Bank analysts said oil would face more downward pressure without escalation in the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal reported.

stories.headline: Mamdani-backed candidates win House seats in New York City
stories.summary: Democratic Socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier won the Bronx's 13th District, along with Ocasio-Cortez and Ritchie Torres in neighboring Bronx races, amNY reported. Gothamist said Mayor Mamdani had endorsed Claire Valdez, Brad Lander and Avila Chevalier, and treated their wins as a sign of his politics' popularity. stories.why_it_matters: New York's delegation in Washington shifts left, which could matter for federal funding fights over transit and housing. It also sets up tests for Hochul and Mamdani within the Democratic Party.
stories.background: Mamdani, a democratic socialist, took office as mayor in January. In this cycle he endorsed several challengers for House seats in New York City. Outlets disagreed on how to read the results: Gothamist called it a signal of his popularity, while the Post called it an extreme-left takeover attempt on the Democratic Party.

facts.text: Avila Chevalier won the 13th Congressional District; amNY said Ocasio-Cortez and Torres also won Bronx seats.

stories.headline: Brooklyn jogger stabbed on waterfront dies; search for attacker continues
stories.summary: Katie Suarez, a jogger stabbed in Brooklyn on Oct. 30, died at NYU Langone Brooklyn, her family announced Tuesday, the Brooklyn Paper reported. The search for the attacker continues. The Daily News reported the death as well.
stories.why_it_matters: A killing of a runner on a public waterfront path with no suspect in custody worries people who use Brooklyn's paths, especially after dark.
stories.background: Suarez was attacked while running on Oct. 30. The Brooklyn Paper described the attack as shocking and mysterious. Her mother told several outlets she died of her injuries days later. No arrest was reported in the digest.

facts.text: Suarez died of her injuries at NYU Langone Brooklyn, her family announced Tuesday.

markets.summary: US stocks were mixed in the latest data: the S&P 500 slipped 0.5% and the Dow 0.4%, while the Nasdaq rose 0.8%. Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal reported that stock futures dipped as Democratic wins came in, then recovered after Trump said he would accept the results. Treasury yields and the dollar fell and gold rose above $4,000 an ounce, per Bloomberg. Analysts quoted by the Financial Times said a divided government lowers the risk of sweeping policy changes. Oil eased toward $103 a barrel on an unconfirmed report of Middle East diplomacy, and euro zone inflation reached 4%, which keeps rate rises in view.

movers.name: Nasdaq Composite
movers.why: Rose 0.8% while the S&P 500 and Dow fell; business reports tied part of the day's tech strength to AMD's earnings, though the digest does not link the index move to one cause.

movers.name: 10-year Treasury yield
movers.why: The 10-year Treasury yield fell 3 basis points to 4.91%, in line with Bloomberg's report of lower yields after the election results.

movers.name: Crude oil (Brent)
movers.why: Brent crude fell 3.9% to $123.10 in the latest reading (Oct. 27); the Financial Times reported oil easing on an unconfirmed report of Middle East diplomacy.

movers.name: Inflation (CPI, year over year)
movers.why: Annual US inflation read 3.72%, up 0.36 percentage point, the largest jump on the board; the digest does not say what drove it.

concept.explanation: Divided government means one party holds the White House while the other controls at least one chamber of Congress. With both chambers flipping to Democrats while Trump stays president, large tax, spending or regulatory changes become harder to pass, because both sides must agree. Investors often read that as lower policy risk, which analysts cited in explaining the calm market reaction. It reaches your wallet through things like tariffs, taxes and government funding fights: sweeping changes become less likely, but standoffs such as budget deadlines can become more likely.

quotes.blurb: The overnight rate the Federal Reserve targets. Every other US interest rate keys off it.

quotes.blurb: What the US government pays to borrow for 2 years. Moves with expectations for Fed rate changes.

quotes.blurb: The government's 10-year borrowing cost. Mortgage rates and company borrowing costs follow it.

quotes.blurb: How much consumer prices rose over the past year. The Fed aims for about 2%.

quotes.name: Unemployment rate
quotes.blurb: Share of people looking for work who can't find it. From the monthly jobs report.

quotes.name: Crude oil (WTI)
quotes.blurb: US oil price per barrel. Feeds into gas prices and inflation.

quotes.name: US dollar index (broad)
quotes.blurb: The Fed's index of the dollar against the currencies of US trading partners. Up means a stronger dollar.

quotes.name: Euro (USD per EUR)

quotes.name: Japanese yen (JPY per USD)
